en: The Sūtra on the Five Things Without Repayment, spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the kingdom of Rājagṛha who heard that the people of Śrāvastī were compassionate, filial, and obedient; that they honored the sutras and cultivated the Way, and made offerings to the Three Honored Ones. He then traveled to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He saw a father and son plowing a field when a venomous snake bit and killed the son; yet the father continued to plow without looking at his son, nor did he weep.
The brahmin asked, "Whose son is this?"
He replied, "This is my son.
The brahmin said:
"This son of yours—why does he not weep and cry, yet plows as before?
The man replied, "In human life there is death;
when things are formed, they must decay. The good receive their retribution, and the evil meet their counterparts. What can sorrow, anxiety, or weeping accomplish? They can pursue nothing."
"If he does not eat or drink, what benefit would it be to the deceased?
You shall enter the city now; my house is at such-and-such a place. I pray you, pass by and tell him:
'Your son is already dead; there is no need to bring food for two people.'"
The brahmin thought to himself:
"This man has no sense of gratitude; though his son lies dead upon the ground, he feels no grief or sorrow, yet instead seeks food.
This man lacks compassion; there is no one to compare with him."
The brahmin then proceeded into the city and went to the house of the plowman; seeing the mother of the deceased child, he immediately said to her:
"Your son is already dead; his father said, 'Bring food for only one person.'"
"Why do you not think of your son?
The mother of the child replied to the brahmin with a parable:
"A son is like a guest; he comes and stays with a person, yet when he comes he is not rejected, and when he departs he is not detained."

This child was originally not summoned by me, yet he came of his own accord while I was alive; he shall likewise depart of his own accord when I die. His advance and retreat are not within my power; they follow his own past karma and pursue the destiny of his birth.
He spoke again to his sister, saying, "Your brother is already dead; why do you not weep?
The sister then addressed the brahmin with a parable:

"We brothers are like master craftsmen who enter the mountains to fell timber and bind it together into a raft upon the water. Suddenly encountering a great wind, the raft is blown apart and scattered, drifting with the current; we are separated from one another, neither looking back nor waiting for the others."
It is the same with my younger brother; due to such karmic conditions from past lives, we have come together at this one time to be born into the same family.
According to the length of our lifespans, death is impermanent; where there is meeting, there must be parting.
"When my younger brother’s life has ended, each must follow their own path; when impermanence confronts one, one follows according to one's original karma and cannot save another.
He then said to the deceased man’s wife, "Your husband is already dead; why do you not weep?"
The wife again spoke a parable for the brahmin, saying:
"We, husband and wife, have met through the convergence of causes and conditions, but this shall last but a moment.
It is like birds that fly at dusk to roost in a high tree; they clamor and chatter together, yet as dawn approaches, each flies away separately to seek food and drink."
When conditions exist, they unite; when conditions cease, they separate. It is thus for husband and wife: when impermanence arrives, each follows their own karmic destiny and cannot save one another.
He further said to his slave, "Your master's son has died; why do you not weep?
The slave then spoke a parable:

"My great master has met with his end through the convergence of causes and conditions. I am like a calf following a great bull; when people slaughter the great bull, the calf remains by its side, unable to save it."
"Life is impermanent and cannot be saved; what is the use of grieving, worrying, or weeping? It will bring no benefit.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin’s mind became bewildered and his vision grew dark; he could no longer distinguish east from west, thinking:
"I heard that the people of this country are filial and obedient, honoring the Way and serving the Three Honored Ones. That is why I have come from afar, desiring to study and learn."
"Since there has been no favorable response, I see that these five men have no sense of reciprocity.
They have exhausted their bodies and minds to come this far, yet it is entirely without benefit.
He then asked the traveler:
"Where is the Buddha?
I wish to go and question him.
The traveler replied:
"He is currently at the Jeta Grove Monastery.
The brahmin immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet in salutation, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Dejected and with his head bowed, he remained silent without saying a word.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, said to the brahmin:
"Why do you lower your head, sorrowful and unhappy?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My wishes have not been fulfilled, which contradicts my original intention; for this reason, I am sorrowful and anxious.
The Buddha asked, "What have you lost?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I have come from the kingdom of Rājagṛha. Having heard that the people of this country are filial and obedient, and revere and honor the Triple Gem, I have traveled from afar wishing to study and inquire.”
"Having come here, I see these five people who lack a sense of reciprocity; therefore, I am sorrowful and find no joy.
The Buddha asked, "What do you mean by 'those who lack a sense of reciprocity'?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha:

"I saw two people, father and son, plowing the earth and sowing seeds; yet when the son died upon the ground, the father felt no grief, but instead went about seeking food and even spoke to me of impermanence.
His mother, his wife, his sister, and the slave were all entirely without sorrow."
"This constitutes a grave rebellion, and there is no possibility of repentance.
The Buddha said, "It is not so; it is not as you say."
These five persons are the most steadfast; knowing that life is impermanent and beyond the reach of sorrow and anxiety, they remain composed and free from grief.
Ordinary people of the world, however, do not recognize impermanence; they wail and weep in anguish, unable to master themselves.
It is like a person who contracts a feverish illness and is unaware of it, speaking deliriously in a daze.
When a skilled physician gives them medicine, the fever is immediately eliminated and cured, and they no longer speak deliriously.
Ordinary people are deluded; they grieve and weep, unable to liberate themselves.
One who can understand impermanence no longer grieves, like one whose feverish illness has been cured. These five persons all attained realization of the Path.
Upon hearing these words of the Buddha, the brahmin immediately reproached himself:
"I have been foolish and deluded, failing to recognize the meaning of the Path.
Now that I have heard the Buddha’s words, it is as if a blind man has regained his sight, seeing light within the darkness."
The Sūtra on the Five Things for Which There Is No Reciprocity Spoken by the Buddha.
